summaries.gardner: Equinix is the top dog in interconnection and a long-term winner (dividend-adjusted price up from about $247 at end-2015 to about $968), riding cloud and AI demand. It falls short of a classic Rule Breaker because it is a capital-heavy REIT founded in 1998, run by a hired CEO, rather than a young disruptive company with a visionary founder.
summaries.buffett: It has a real moat (network effects and switching costs, MRR churn around 2%) and recurring revenue, which Buffett likes. But returns on capital are low (ROIC about 5.6%), free cash flow is negative after growth capex, debt and leases are about $22 billion, and the shares trade at about 62 times trailing earnings, so it is a weak fit.
summaries.munger: Munger would admire the lollapalooza of network effects inside its buildings, but dislike the heavy capital needs, leverage and a valuation that leaves little margin for error. Inverting, the main ways to fail are overbuilding, funding stress if rates rise, or hyperscalers bypassing it.
summaries.lynch: Equinix is a stalwart with fast-grower traits: revenue has risen every year and 2026 is guided up 11-12%. Lynch would like the simple story but balk at a P/E of about 62 against EPS growth near 10-15%, the rising share count and full Wall Street coverage.
summaries.fisher: Fisher's points on market potential, sales strength (4,500+ deals in Q4 2025, record bookings) and long-term outlook fit well. Weaker spots are modest profit margins after depreciation, frequent equity issuance that dilutes owners, and no disclosed R&D engine.
summaries.graham: It fails Graham's defensive tests: P/E around 62, price-to-book about 6.6, dividends only since its 2015 REIT conversion, and debt well above current assets. It does pass on size, ten years of profits and EPS growth (from $1.79 in 2016 to $13.76 in 2025).
summaries.thiel: Equinix built a near-monopoly position in neutral interconnection, starting small in 1998 and expanding to over 500,000 interconnections, and has strong distribution. It lacks 10x proprietary technology, and the AI data center opportunity is visible to many well-funded rivals.
summaries.gerstner: Gerstner would see a clear beneficiary of AI infrastructure demand with accelerating bookings (up 27% in 2025) and a 2027-2029 outlook of 10-13% revenue growth. He would weigh that against a full valuation, low free cash flow and a stock that has only kept pace with the market over the past year.
summaries.druckenmiller: The story is improving: guidance was raised, AFFO per share grew 18% in Q2 2026 and AI demand is strong, which suits a liquidity-and-earnings-momentum trader. But the stock is sensitive to interest rates and fell after a soft Q3 revenue outlook, so conviction for a big position is limited.
summaries.smith: Terry Smith wants high returns on capital, high margins and strong cash conversion; Equinix's ROIC of about 5.6%, gross margin of 51% and negative free cash flow after expansion capex miss those tests. Its durable, recurring business is good but it does not look like a Fundsmith-style compounder at today's price.
summaries.greenblatt: On the Magic Formula, Equinix scores poorly: operating income of about $2.1 billion over the last twelve months is under 2% of its roughly $118 billion enterprise value, and return on capital is low because of its huge property base.
summaries.akre: Akre's stool: the business is good with a moat, and management is competent, but the reinvestment leg relies on debt and new shares rather than free cash flow. Stabilized assets earning about 27% cash-on-cash yields show strong unit returns, so it is a partial fit.
summaries.pabrai: Pabrai seeks simple businesses in temporary distress bought at deep discounts with low downside. Equinix is simple and durable but not distressed or cheap, so the Dhandho 'heads I win, tails I don't lose much' setup is absent.
summaries.wood: Equinix is an enabler of AI and cloud rather than a disruptive innovator on ARK's platforms. Its costs do not fall rapidly with scale and its market is growing about 10-13% a year, not the exponential curve ARK looks for.
summaries.ackman: Ackman likes simple, predictable, free-cash-flow-generative businesses with high barriers to entry. Equinix is simple, predictable and protected, but its free cash flow is negative while it builds, and its leverage and capital intensity cut against his criteria.
summaries.sleep: Nick Sleep's 'scale economies shared' model fits only partly: Equinix reinvests and its network grows more valuable as it grows, but it does not visibly pass scale savings back to customers through lower prices; instead it relies on firm pricing.
summaries.valentine: Valentine looked for huge markets and products solving painful problems. Equinix serves a large, essential need (connecting clouds, networks and AI) but is a mature public company, not an early-stage venture bet.
summaries.nash: Equinix sells real infrastructure into the AI and cloud trend and scores well on moat, secular trend and ownership quality. It fails Nash's balance-sheet rules (debt far above cash, negative free cash flow, interest coverage under 4x) and his valuation tests, so it scores as a quality business at a stretched price.

momentum.evidence: EQIX rose about 15.3% over the 52 weeks to Oct 26, 2026 ($967.65), roughly matching SPY's 14.2% total return, and is well below its 52-week high of $1,128.68.

g4.evidence: Sovereign fund GIC and CPP Investments are partners in its planned $15 billion-plus US xScale joint venture, and CEO Adaire Fox-Martin previously ran go-to-market at Google Cloud.

g6.evidence: Some commentators flag its P/E of about 62, but most of 34 analysts rate it Buy with an average $1,233 price target.

simple.evidence: It rents data center space, power and cross-connects on recurring contracts; 95% of 2025 revenue ($8,739M of $9,217M) was recurring.

b2.evidence: Revenue grew every year from $5,999M in 2020 to $9,217M in 2025, and diluted EPS was positive every year from 2015 to 2025.

integrity.evidence: Hindenburg's 2024 report accused it of inflating AFFO; an audit committee review found no restatement was needed and the SEC closed its probe in November 2025, but pay tied to AFFO drew criticism.

b6.evidence: It funds hyperscale growth through capital-light xScale joint ventures with GIC and CPP Investments rather than on its own balance sheet, though it has a long history of acquisitions.

roic.evidence: ROIC is about 5.6% and ROE about 10.7% (StockAnalysis, Oct 2026), supported by debt-to-equity of about 1.6.

fcf.evidence: In 2025 operating cash flow of $3,911M was outrun by $5,305M of PP&E and real estate purchases, so free cash flow was about -$1.4B, though AFFO was $3,761M.

b10.evidence: As a REIT it pays out most cash ($1,856M of dividends in 2025) and raises equity; market value has grown, but much of the growth was funded with new shares and debt.

safety.evidence: At $967.65 it trades at about 62 times trailing EPS and about 22.5 times the 2026 AFFO guidance midpoint (about $43), with no clear discount to conservative value.

fairprice.evidence: About 22.5 times 2026 AFFO for 9-12% AFFO per share growth guided through 2029 is reasonable for a REIT of its quality, though not cheap.

mu5.evidence: Sticky, interconnected customers make collapse unlikely, but $22 billion of debt and leases, heavy capex and AI overbuilding risk give it some ways to stumble.

reinvest.evidence: Its 194 stabilized assets earn about a 27% cash-on-cash yield and it has 52 major projects underway in 33 markets, giving years of high-return reinvestment.

ly2.evidence: It is a stalwart: the leading interconnection landlord growing revenue 10-13% a year through 2029 as AI and cloud traffic grows.

ly3.evidence: Trailing P/E is about 62 and forward P/E about 56, far above earnings growth of roughly 10-20%.

runway.evidence: It controls about 3 GW of land and power with about 700 MW under construction and guides 10-13% annual revenue growth through 2029.

ly7.evidence: The share count rose about 1.4% over the past year and diluted shares grew from 88.4M in 2020 to 99.1M in Q2 2026; no notable insider buying was found.

ly8.evidence: About 34 analysts cover it and institutions own about 99.7% of the shares.

fi2.evidence: It keeps adding products such as Fabric Cloud Router (bookings up 170% year over year in Q2 2026), Fabric Geo Zones and xScale AI campuses.

fi3.evidence: Equinix does not report R&D spending separately, so its productivity cannot be measured.

fi4.evidence: It closed more than 4,500 deals in Q4 2025 and record annualized gross bookings of $1.6 billion in 2025, up 27%.

longterm.evidence: It plans $5-7 billion of capex a year through 2029 and accepts negative free cash flow now to build long-lived capacity.

gr1.evidence: Market cap is about $95 billion and 2025 revenue was $9.2 billion.

ni10.evidence: Diluted EPS was positive every year from 2016 ($1.79) to 2025 ($13.76).

gr4.evidence: Equinix began paying regular dividends in 2015 after converting to a REIT, about 11 years.

eps10.evidence: Diluted EPS rose from $3.21 in 2015 to $13.76 in 2025.

gr6.evidence: The price is about 62 times trailing EPS, far above 15 times average earnings.

gr7.evidence: P/E of about 62 times P/B of about 6.6 gives roughly 400, far above 22.5.

th1.evidence: Its edge is network density and locations, not technology ten times better than Digital Realty's or NTT's.

timing.evidence: AI drove about 60% of its largest Q4 2025 deals, and 8 of the top 10 AI model providers run networking on Equinix.

th3.evidence: Founded in 1998 to run neutral internet exchange points, it dominated that niche and expanded to about 280 data centers on six continents.

team.evidence: CEO Adaire Fox-Martin brings Google Cloud and SAP experience but has led Equinix only since 2024.

th5.evidence: It has a global direct sales force and partner channel and a self-serve Fabric portal, serving more than 10,500 customers.

durable.evidence: Networks keep clustering where others already are, and its interconnection lead has held for over two decades.

th7.evidence: Its neutral, multi-cloud interconnection hub idea was unique early on, but AI data center demand is now obvious to everyone.

trend.evidence: It benefits from cloud and AI: MRR grew 11% and bookings 23% in Q2 2026, with AI workloads driving large deals.

dr1.evidence: AFFO per share rose 18% in Q2 2026 and 2026 AFFO per share guidance moved from $41.93-42.74 in February to $42.69-43.29 in July.

dr2.evidence: About 700 MW under construction and xScale JV deployments should lift results by 2028, but much of this is already in guidance.

dr4.evidence: As a leveraged REIT ($22 billion of debt and leases), it gains from falling rates and loses from rising ones, while the economy matters less given recurring revenue.

dr6.evidence: Q3 2026 results on Oct 28, 2026, further xScale lease signings and AI inference deployments could lift results.

dr7.evidence: Capital intensity, leverage and a high valuation make it hard to justify as a large concentrated position.

gm.evidence: Gross margin was 51.1% in 2025, decent for real estate but far below software-like levels.

fcfyield.evidence: Reported free cash flow yield is about -2.7%, but AFFO yield is about 4.4% (about $43 of 2026 AFFO per share on $967.65).

pa2.evidence: The business is not in a setback; revenue rose 16% in Q2 2026 and guidance was raised.

pa4.evidence: With recurring revenue, 1.8% quarterly churn and assets in prime metros, permanent loss of capital is unlikely, though valuation compression could hurt.

wo2.evidence: Data center building and power costs are rising, not falling quickly with volume.
